content.content:
# Postmark — transactional email for Next.js Postmark sends an app's transactional email (welcome emails, password resets, receipts) with high delivery rates, bounce and spam processing, and detailed statistics. The official Node.js library `postmark` covers the whole Postmark REST API, uses the native Fetch API and has no runtime dependencies (Node 18+). ## Install ```bash npm install postmark ``` ## 1. Environment variables `.env.local`: ``` POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN=server_token_placeholder POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL=hello@example.com ``` The server token belongs to one Postmark server (Servers → API Tokens). The From address must be a confirmed sender signature or sit on a verified domain. ## 2. Create a client `src/lib/postmark.ts`: ```ts import { ServerClient } from "postmark"; export const postmark = new ServerClient(process.env.POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN!); ``` Use the client only in server code (route handlers, server actions, server components). Never expose the server token to the browser. ## 3. Send an email ```ts import { postmark } from "@/lib/postmark"; await postmark.sendEmail({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", Subject: "Welcome!", HtmlBody: "

Thanks for signing up.

", TextBody: "Thanks for signing up.", MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `outbound` is the default transactional message stream. Keep transactional and broadcast email in separate streams. ## 4. Send with a template Create the template once in the Postmark dashboard, then send it by alias: ```ts await postmark.sendEmailWithTemplate({ From: process.env.POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL!, To: "user@example.com", TemplateAlias: "password-reset", TemplateModel: { name: "Ada", action_url: "https://example.com/reset?token=..." }, MessageStream: "outbound", }); ``` `TemplateId` (a number) works in place of `TemplateAlias`. ## 5. Handle errors `sendEmail` returns a promise that rejects with a typed error from `postmark`'s `Errors` export when Postmark refuses the message (inactive recipient, unconfirmed sender, invalid token). Catch it where the email is triggered so a failed email does not break the request that caused it. ## Why teams pick Postmark - Built for transactional email: high delivery rates, with bounce and spam handling included. - Templates live in the dashboard, so copy changes do not need a deploy. - Detailed delivery statistics and inbound email parsing come with the same account. # env files (can opt-in for committing if needed) .env* next-env.d.ts import { getCurrentUser, listUsers } from "@/lib/users"; export default async function DashboardPage() { const me = await getCurrentUser(); const all = await listUsers(); return (

Dashboard

Signed in as {me?.name ?? "nobody"} ({me?.email ?? "—"})

Team

    {all.map((u) => (
  • {u.name} — {u.email} — joined {u.createdAt}
    • ))}
); }

content.text:
Notely now sends a welcome email when a user is created and a password reset email when one is requested, using **Postmark**. The build and lint pass. A test run against Postmark's real API reached it, but with the placeholder token Postmark refused to send (401 invalid token, as expected), so no email has actually been delivered yet. That run did confirm three things: the user is still created when the email fails, the error is logged, and a made-up reset token is rejected.

**Why Postmark:** it only does transactional email and is known for reliable delivery to the inbox. It handles bounces and spam complaints for you, and its official Node library has no other dependencies. The repo already had Postmark docs in `docs/postmark.md`, and I followed their setup.

**What changed**
- **`src/lib/postmark.ts`**: the Postmark connection. It's created the first time an email is sent, so a missing token causes an error at send time rather than crashing the app on startup. It's marked server-only so the token can't end up in browser code.
- **`src/lib/email.ts`**: `sendWelcomeEmail` and `sendPasswordResetEmail`. Each sends both an HTML and a plain-text version and is tagged so you can see its stats separately in Postmark. User names are escaped before going into the HTML, and links are built from `APP_URL`. I wrote the email content in code rather than as Postmark dashboard templates, so it works without any setup in the dashboard.
- **`src/lib/users.ts`** has three new functions:
  - `createUser`: normalizes the email address, refuses duplicates, saves the user, then sends the welcome email. If the email fails, signup still succeeds and the error is logged.
  - `requestPasswordReset(email)`: creates a random reset token that expires after 60 minutes and emails a link to `/reset-password?token=…`. Only a hash of the token is stored, and older tokens for the same user are cancelled. It behaves the same whether or not the email exists, so it can't be used to check which accounts exist.
  - `consumePasswordResetToken(token)`: returns the user if the token is valid, and deletes the token so it works only once.
- **`.env.example`**: `POSTMARK_SERVER_TOKEN`, `POSTMARK_FROM_EMAIL` and `APP_URL`, all with placeholder values. The `.gitignore` rule for `.env*` was also ignoring this file, so I added an exception to let it be committed.
- **Dependencies**: added `postmark` and `server-only`.

**Still to do**
- **No passwords exist yet.** Users don't have a password field, so `consumePasswordResetToken` only works out who the reset is for. Saving the new password depends on whatever login system you add.
- **The reset link points to a page that doesn't exist.** There's no `/reset-password` page or signup form yet; I only built what the existing user code needed.
- **Data is lost on restart.** Users and reset tokens are kept in memory, the same way the existing user list is. They'll move to the database along with users.
- **Before emails will send:** set a real Postmark server token, and confirm the From address in Postmark (either as a sender signature or on a verified domain).

`npx tsc --noEmit` shows an error about `LayoutProps` in `src/app/layout.tsx`. That error was already in the starter project; `next build` generates that type and builds cleanly. I haven't committed anything.
